handsOnLab.title: Detection statistics toolkit in Python

mockTask.q: Panel question: a vendor pitches an IDS with '99% accuracy.' What do you ask before it touches your network?

notes.body:
All of detection is conditional probability, so we start with the foundations and make them operational. A sample space is the set of all possible outcomes; an event is a subset. P(A) is the fraction of the space where A happens. Conditional probability P(A|B) — 'probability of A given B' — is the fraction of B-outcomes where A also holds: P(A|B) = P(A∧B)/P(B). Worked: a SOC sees 10,000 network events; 200 are port scans (event S), and 50 of those come from external addresses (event E∧S). P(E|S) = 50/200 = 0.25 — a quarter of scans are external. Note the direction matters: P(S|E) — 'given external, how many are scans' — is a different number requiring the count of external events. Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A) is the prosecutor's fallacy wearing a SOC badge: '99% of intrusions trigger this alert' (P(alert|intrusion)) is not '99% of alerts are intrusions' (P(intrusion|alert)) — the second is what the analyst needs, and it is usually far smaller. Independence: A and B are independent if P(A∧B) = P(A)P(B) — knowing one tells you nothing about the other. Worked: two independent sensors each with 1% false-positive rate. P(both false-positive) = 0.01×0.01 = 0.0001 — independent corroboration multiplies confidence, which is why defense-in-depth stacks independent signals. But verify independence: two signatures from the same vendor on the same engine are not independent — correlated sensors give correlated failures, and the multiplication is a lie. The law of total probability partitions the space: P(A) = P(A|M)P(M) + P(A|¬M)P(¬M) — 'alerts come from malicious events plus benign events,' the denominator you will need for Bayes. Common mistake: treating 'rare' as 'never.' A 0.1% event across a million daily events happens a thousand times a day. Scale converts rarity into routine — the fundamental reason SOC math surprises newcomers.

The prosecutor's fallacy deserves its own worked autopsy because it recurs in incident response. Setup: 1% of employees are malicious insiders (prior). A UEBA tool flags 90% of malicious insiders (P(flag|malicious) = 0.9) and 8% of benign employees (P(flag|benign) = 0.08). An employee is flagged. P(malicious|flag) = (0.9 x 0.01) / (0.9 x 0.01 + 0.08 x 0.99) = 0.009 / (0.009 + 0.0792) = 0.009 / 0.0882, about 10.2%. The tool is '90% accurate at catching insiders' and the flagged employee is roughly 10% likely to be one. Presenting the 90% number to HR as the employee's guilt probability is the fallacy — and it ruins lives when the base rate is ignored in personnel decisions. The correct presentation: 'the flag raises the probability from 1% to 10% — investigate, don't accuse.' Every detection number you report must survive this translation: what was the prior, what is the posterior, and what action does the posterior justify? Investigation thresholds and accusation thresholds are different numbers, and Bayes tells you which is which.
notes.title: Probability foundations for detection

notes.body:
Bayes' theorem is the single most important equation in security operations: it converts 'how good is the sensor' into 'how much should I believe this alert.' P(M|A) = P(A|M)·P(M) / P(A), where P(A) = P(A|M)P(M) + P(A|¬M)P(¬M). In words: posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence. The prior P(M) is the base rate — how often malicious events occur. The likelihood P(A|M) is the sensor's true-positive rate. The denominator counts all alerts, true and false. Worked — the IDS example, every number shown. Setup: 1% of events are malicious (prior P(M)=0.01). The detector catches 99% of malicious events (P(A|M)=0.99) and false-alarms on 5% of benign events (P(A|¬M)=0.05). An alert fires. How likely is it real? Numerator: P(A|M)·P(M) = 0.99 × 0.01 = 0.0099. Denominator: 0.0099 + P(A|¬M)·P(¬M) = 0.0099 + 0.05×0.99 = 0.0099 + 0.0495 = 0.0594. Posterior: 0.0099/0.0594 = 1/6 ≈ 0.1667. Sixteen point seven percent. A '99% accurate' detector produces alerts that are real one time in six — because the 5% false-positive rate applies to the 99% of traffic that is benign, generating far more false alerts than the 1% malicious base generates true ones. Frequency form, same result, more intuitive: 10,000 events → 100 malicious, 9,900 benign. Detector flags 99 of the 100 malicious and 5% of 9,900 = 495 benign. Total alerts: 594. Real: 99. 99/594 = 16.7%. Teach the frequency form to stakeholders; keep the formula for yourself. The lesson: sensor quality (likelihood) and alert believability (posterior) are different things, joined by the base rate. Every 'why are all our alerts false positives' complaint is Bayes' theorem asking to be noticed. Common mistake: quoting the true-positive rate as the alert's credibility. P(A|M)=99% does not mean the alert is 99% likely real — that confusion is the base-rate fallacy, next note.

Bayes composes: each new piece of evidence updates the posterior, which becomes the next prior. The IDS alert took us from 1% to 16.7%. Now a second, independent sensor — say, a sandbox detonation — also flags the file, with its own 90% TP and 5% FP. Update: prior 0.1667, posterior = (0.9 x 0.1667) / (0.9 x 0.1667 + 0.05 x 0.8333) = 0.15 / (0.15 + 0.0417) = 0.15 / 0.1917, about 78.3%. Two mediocre sensors in agreement: 78% — the independence multiplies the evidence. (Verify independence before multiplying: two signatures from the same engine don't count twice.) This is the mathematical form of 'corroborate before you escalate': each independent confirmation should move your belief by a computed amount, not by vibes. In practice, run the SOC on posterior tiers: single-sensor alerts get automated enrichment, two-sensor agreement gets analyst review, three get immediate escalation. The tier boundaries are posterior thresholds you have computed, not alert counts someone guessed. And log the updates — when the post-incident review asks 'why did you escalate,' the answer is a chain of Bayesian updates, each with its numbers. That is defensible triage.
notes.title: Bayes' theorem, worked on IDS alerts

notes.body:
The base-rate fallacy is ignoring the prior — and in security, the prior is always tiny, so ignoring it is always catastrophic. Restate the IDS result as a fallacy autopsy: the analyst hears '99% detection rate, 5% false positives' and feels the alert is ~99% likely real. The actual answer is 16.7%. The missing ingredient was the base rate: malicious events are 1% of traffic, so the false positives (5% of the huge benign mass) swamp the true positives (99% of the tiny malicious sliver). Now scale it to a real SOC and watch it get worse. Worked: 1,000,000 events per day, 10 real attacks (base rate 0.001%). Same excellent sensor: 99% TP, 1% FP. True alerts: 10 × 0.99 = 9.9. False alerts: 999,990 × 0.01 = 9,999.9. Total: ~10,010 alerts per day, of which ~10 are real. Precision: 9.9/10,009.8 ≈ 0.099% — one alert in a thousand is real. The sensor is superb and the alert stream is 99.9% noise. This is not a sensor problem; it is arithmetic. Operational consequences, in order of leverage. First, tune thresholds per environment: the vendor's default threshold was set for their demo data, not your base rate — measure precision on your traffic and move the threshold until the alert volume is triageable. Second, stack independent signals: two independent 1%-FPR sensors ANDed give 0.01% FPR on the combination (independence permitting), which is how you dig out of the base-rate hole. Third, enrich before alerting: an alert with asset context, threat intel, and corroborating logs is a different (higher-prior) population than a raw signature hit — tier your response by posterior, not by sensor output. Fourth, accept the math publicly: tell stakeholders 'our IDS alerts are 15% likely real, which is why every alert gets corroboration' — managing expectations beats apologizing for false positives. Common mistake: 'fixing' the base-rate problem by buying a 'more accurate' sensor. Going from 99% to 99.9% TP barely moves the posterior; cutting the false-positive rate in half doubles it. When base rates are tiny, false-positive rate is the only metric that matters.

The base rate is not a single number — it varies by population, and stratifying is free precision. The 0.001% base rate was across all events; but among events already flagged by a coarse pre-filter, or from high-risk assets, or during an active campaign, the prior is much higher. Worked: take the SOC example but restrict to alerts from the finance VLAN during a known phishing campaign — suppose the prior there is 2%. Same sensor (99% TP, 1% FP): posterior = (0.99 x 0.02) / (0.99 x 0.02 + 0.01 x 0.98) = 0.0198 / (0.0198 + 0.0098) = 0.0198 / 0.0296, about 66.9%. Identical sensor, 0.1% to 67% believability, purely from a better prior. Operationalize this: tier your alerting by population priors — exec assets, crown-jewel servers, and campaign-targeted groups get lower thresholds because their base rates justify it; the general population gets higher thresholds. This is also why threat intel matters mathematically: intel doesn't just add detections, it raises priors on specific populations, making every sensor more precise there. 'Context' in SOC-speak is often just 'a better prior' in statistics-speak — and now you can compute exactly how much better.
notes.title: The base-rate fallacy in alerting

notes.body:
Precision, recall, and F1 are the working vocabulary for evaluating any detector — learn them as ratios on the confusion matrix, not as slogans. The matrix: rows are ground truth (actually malicious / actually benign), columns are the detector's verdict (flagged / not flagged). Four cells: TP (true positives — caught badness), FP (false positives — false alarms), FN (false negatives — missed badness), TN (true negatives — correctly ignored). Precision = TP/(TP+FP): of everything flagged, how much was real — the analyst's 'is this alert worth my time' number. Recall = TP/(TP+FN): of all real badness, how much was caught — also called true-positive rate or sensitivity. FPR = FP/(FP+TN): of benign events, how many false-alarmed. Worked on a concrete matrix — TP=90, FP=30, FN=10, TN=870 (1,000 events, 100 actually malicious). Precision = 90/(90+30) = 90/120 = 0.75. Recall = 90/(90+10) = 90/100 = 0.9. F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R) = 2(0.75)(0.9)/(0.75+0.9) = 1.35/1.65 ≈ 0.818. F1 is the harmonic mean — it punishes lopsided tradeoffs: precision 1.0 with recall 0.01 gives F1 ≈ 0.02, exposing the 'flag nothing, be precisely right' cheat that accuracy would hide. (Accuracy here would be (90+870)/1000 = 96% — sounds great, misses 10% of attacks.) The tradeoff is fundamental: lowering the threshold catches more (recall up) but alarms more (precision down, FPR up). There is no threshold with both perfect — the detector's quality is the whole tradeoff curve, which is the ROC of the next note. Choose the operating point economically: estimate the cost of a false positive (analyst minutes) and a false negative (breach risk), and pick the threshold minimizing expected cost — not the threshold maximizing F1, unless your costs happen to be symmetric. Common mistake: reporting accuracy on imbalanced data. The M25 vendor demolition ('99.9% accurate, 0% recall') is the canonical example — accuracy is the metric you quote when you want to hide the tradeoff.

Choose the metric by the decision it informs. Tuning a threshold? Watch precision and recall move against each other and pick the economic optimum. Comparing two detectors for purchase? Compare full ROC curves, not single points — a detector that wins at your operating region is what matters. Reporting to leadership? Precision ('what fraction of analyst hours were well spent') and alert volume, because that is the budget they feel. Hunting false negatives? Recall on a labeled set, because precision is silent about misses. Debugging a bad week? The confusion matrix itself — which cell grew tells you what changed (FP spike means benign traffic shifted or the threshold drifted; FN spike means the attacker adapted or there is a coverage gap). And never let anyone optimize accuracy on your imbalanced data — the vendor demolition stands. One more: when classes are imbalanced, also report the raw counts alongside ratios. 'Precision 0.75' could be 3/4 or 750/1000 — the ratio is the same, the evidence behind it isn't. Ratios summarize; counts justify. Give both, always.
notes.title: Precision, recall, F1: reading the confusion matrix

notes.body:
A ROC curve shows the detector's entire tradeoff surface: true-positive rate (recall) on the vertical axis versus false-positive rate on the horizontal, traced as the threshold sweeps from 'flag everything' (top-right: TPR=1, FPR=1) to 'flag nothing' (bottom-left: 0,0). A perfect detector hugs the top-left corner (TPR=1 at FPR=0); a random detector is the diagonal (flagging at random catches badness exactly as often as it false-alarms). Real detectors bow toward the top-left, and the area under the curve (AUC) summarizes the bow in one number: 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is coin-flip. Worked intuition with the synthetic example from your lab: benign scores cluster around 0, malicious around 2 (both with spread 1). At threshold 1.0 you catch most malicious (high TPR) with moderate false alarms; at threshold 3.0 you almost never false-alarm (low FPR) but miss much malicious (low TPR). The ROC is the curve connecting these operating points — and moving the threshold slides you along it, never off it. Two honest uses. First, comparing detectors: if detector A's ROC is everywhere above B's, A is better at every tradeoff — no threshold games can rescue B. If the curves cross, the 'better' detector depends on your operating region (low-FPR region for SOC triage, high-TPR region for pre-breach hunting). Second, choosing the operating point: mark your cost ratio on the curve — the optimal threshold is where the marginal true positive is worth the marginal false positives. AUC's honest limit: it averages over all thresholds including absurd ones (FPR=0.9 is not an operating point anyone uses), so for SOC work, partial AUC over the low-FPR region is the serious metric. Common mistake: 'our model has 0.99 AUC' as a deployment argument. AUC measures ranking quality across thresholds; your deployment lives at one threshold, on your base rate, with your costs. Report the confusion matrix at the operating threshold — AUC is the trailer, not the movie.

For imbalanced detection problems, the precision-recall (PR) curve is often more honest than ROC. ROC's FPR uses true negatives in the denominator — and when benign events number in the millions, the FPR stays tiny even with thousands of false alarms, making the ROC look deceptively good. The PR curve plots precision vs recall directly: it shows what the analyst experiences (how much of my queue is real?) at each recall level. Worked intuition: our SOC sensor at 99% TP and 1% FP has a fine-looking ROC point (TPR 0.99, FPR 0.01 — near the top-left!) but a PR point of (recall 0.99, precision 0.001) — the PR curve exposes the operational reality the ROC hides. Rule of thumb: balanced classes, use ROC; imbalanced (the security norm), use the PR curve, with area under the PR curve as the summary. Report both when comparing detectors, but make decisions on the PR curve at your operating region. And the same threshold economics apply: pick the PR point where marginal costs balance. The curve changes; the decision method doesn't. Metrics are lenses — choose the lens that shows the thing you are deciding about.
notes.title: ROC curves: the full tradeoff picture

notes.body:
Detection also needs counting statistics: how many events to expect, and whether today's count is weird. Two distributions cover most operational questions. The binomial counts successes in n independent yes/no trials: P(exactly k) = C(n,k)·p^k·(1−p)^(n−k). Worked: 100 logins, each independently 1% likely malicious. P(at least one malicious) = 1 − P(none) = 1 − 0.99^100 ≈ 1 − 0.366 = 0.634. A 1% per-login risk becomes a 63% certainty of at least one bad login in a hundred — scale converts rarity to routine again, the quantitative backbone of 'assume breach.' Expected count: n·p = 1. The Poisson counts events in continuous time or space when they occur at a constant average rate λ, independently: P(k events) = e^(−λ)·λ^k/k!. Worked: port-scan probes arrive at λ=2 per hour. P(0 in an hour) = e^(−2)·2^0/0! = e^(−2) ≈ 0.135 — a quiet hour happens 13.5% of the time, don't celebrate. P(5 in an hour) = e^(−2)·32/120 ≈ 0.036 — five probes in an hour happens 3.6% of the time by pure chance; investigate, but know the base rate of 'weird-looking' hours. The Poisson's signature property: mean = variance = λ. If your observed counts vary much more than λ (variance ≫ mean), the process isn't simple-Poisson — it's bursty or clustered, which itself is signal (botnets beacon in bursts; humans don't). Operational uses: set alert thresholds from the distribution ('alert when hourly count exceeds the 99.9th percentile of Poisson(λ)') instead of from gut feeling; size log pipelines from expected rates plus headroom; and sanity-check vendor 'anomaly' claims — an 'anomalous' burst with 5% Poisson probability is Tuesday, not an incident. The two distributions connect: binomial with large n and small p approaches Poisson with λ=np — the 100-logins example (λ=1) gives P(0)=e^(−1)≈0.368, matching the binomial 0.366. Common mistake: alerting on counts without a rate model. 'Unusually many' is not a finding until you've computed what 'usual' looks like.

The variance check deserves a worked example because it is a detector you can deploy tomorrow. You monitor DNS queries per minute to a rarely-used internal resolver: historical mean lambda = 4 per minute. Under Poisson, variance should also be about 4 (std about 2). This week you observe minute-counts: mean 4.2, variance 38. Variance far above mean — not Poisson. Something is bursty: maybe a misconfigured retry loop, maybe DNS tunneling exfiltrating in bursts. The check caught what the mean missed (the mean barely moved). Formalize it: track the index of dispersion (variance divided by mean); alert when it exceeds, say, 3 for sustained windows. This is a real, deployed technique — simple, explainable, and sensitive to exactly the shaped traffic attackers generate (beacons, bursts, retries). Caveats: legitimate burstiness exists (batch jobs, cron storms) — baseline per-asset and per-hour, and confirm with a second signal before escalating. But as a cheap first-pass anomaly screen over count data, variance-versus-mean is one of the highest-value statistics in the module. It also generalizes: whenever a model assumes a distribution, check the moments. Models fail at the assumptions, and the assumptions are checkable.
notes.title: Binomial and Poisson: counting events like an operator

notes.body:
Close the loop: turn the statistics into a detection-quality program you can run. Four practices. One — characterize every detector with a confusion matrix measured on your data, at your operating threshold, refreshed regularly. Not the vendor's matrix, not last year's matrix: yours, now. Track precision, recall, and F1 over time; a drifting F1 is the earliest warning that the threat landscape or your traffic mix moved. Two — hunt your false negatives deliberately. False positives announce themselves (analysts complain); false negatives are silent. Sample closed-as-benign alerts and re-investigate a random subset deeply; sample raw event streams the detectors never flagged and hunt manually. Estimate the miss rate with a confidence interval and report it alongside precision — a detector with 90% precision and unknown recall is half-characterized. Three — price your thresholds. For each detection tier, write down the cost of a false positive (analyst triage minutes × volume) and the cost model of a false negative (expected breach cost × probability the miss matters). Set thresholds where marginal costs balance, and re-price when volumes change — a threshold that was optimal at 1,000 alerts/day is wrong at 10,000. Four — evaluate like a scientist (M26's experiment discipline applies to detectors too): any new detection logic ships with a baseline comparison, pre-registered metrics, and a rollback criterion. 'We deployed the new rule and alerts went up' is not an evaluation; 'precision held at 0.8 while recall rose from 0.7 to 0.85 on the labeled set' is. Worked program sketch for your IDS: monthly, pull 5,000 labeled events (1,000 malicious from confirmed incidents and red-team activity, 4,000 benign sampled from production); run the current ruleset; publish precision/recall/F1 and the ROC operating point; quarterly, run the false-negative hunt on 200 sampled benign-closed alerts. That is a detection engineering practice, not a tool purchase — and it is what separates teams that detect from teams that alert. Common mistake: treating detection as a product rather than a process. Products decay (M27's arms race); processes adapt. The statistics in this module are the process's instrumentation.

The labeled set is the hard part — labels are expensive, so be systematic about manufacturing them. Three sources. One: confirmed incidents — every resolved incident's indicators become malicious labels, with timestamps bounding the malicious window. Two: red-team and purple-team activity — schedule it partly to generate labels; every red-team action is a known-malicious event with ground truth, the cheapest high-quality labels you will ever get. Three: benign sampling with verification — randomly sample production events and have analysts verify a subset as benign (this is also your false-negative hunt). Maintain the set like code: versioned, with provenance per label (who labeled, from what evidence, when), and refreshed — last year's labels decay as traffic and threats shift. Size guidance: enough malicious samples that a 5-point recall change is statistically meaningful (hundreds, not dozens). And keep a held-out portion the detection engineers never see — evaluate on it, or you are measuring memorization. A detection program without a maintained labeled set is flying blind with extra steps; with one, every tuning decision becomes a measurement.
